hints: Recall that at constant speed, the resistive force equals the driving force produced by the athlete.
Use $P = Fv$ with $P = 60\text{ W}$ and $v = 3\text{ m s}^{-1}$ to solve for the resistive force.
walkthrough:
Relate driving force to power and speed at constant velocity ($a = 0\text{ m s}^{-2}$):
$$R = F = \frac{P}{v} = \frac{60}{3} = 20\text{ N}$$
teacher_walkthrough:
Name the relationship between power, driving force, and speed:
$$P = Fv$$

When running at constant speed, acceleration is zero, so the resistive force $R$ balances the forward driving force $F$:
$$R = F = \frac{P}{v}$$

Substitute $P = 60\text{ W}$ and $v = 3\text{ m s}^{-1}$:
$$R = \frac{60}{3} = 20\text{ N}$$

hints: Calculate the net work done by the driving and resistive forces: $W_{\text{net}} = (24 - 13) \times 150 = 1650\text{ J}$.
Calculate the gain in gravitational potential energy: $\Delta E_p = mgh = 84(10)(150\sin 0.8^\circ)$.
Express the change in kinetic energy: $\Delta E_k = \frac{1}{2}(84)v^2 - \frac{1}{2}(84)(3^2) = 42v^2 - 378$.
Form the work-energy equation $W_{\text{net}} = \Delta E_k + \Delta E_p$ and solve for the final speed $v$.
walkthrough:
Calculate the work done by the driving force and against the resistance force:
$$W_D - W_R = (24 - 13) \times 150 = 11 \times 150 = 1650\text{ J}$$

Calculate the increase in gravitational potential energy:
$$\Delta E_p = mgd\sin 0.8^\circ = 84(10)(150\sin 0.8^\circ) \approx 1759.23\text{ J}$$

Express the change in kinetic energy:
$$\Delta E_k = \frac{1}{2}(84)v^2 - \frac{1}{2}(84)(3)^2 = 42v^2 - 378$$

Apply the work-energy principle and solve for $v$:
$$W_D - W_R = \Delta E_k + \Delta E_p$$
$$1650 = (42v^2 - 378) + 1759.23$$
$$42v^2 = 1650 + 378 - 1759.23 = 268.77$$
$$v^2 = \frac{268.77}{42} \approx 6.399 \implies v \approx 2.53\text{ m s}^{-1}$$
teacher_walkthrough:
Name the work-energy theorem: the net work done by external non-gravitational forces equals the change in kinetic energy plus the change in gravitational potential energy:
$$W_D - W_R = \Delta E_k + \Delta E_p$$

Calculate the work done by the constant driving force $F_D = 24\text{ N}$ over distance $d = 150\text{ m}$:
$$W_D = F_D \times d = 24 \times 150 = 3600\text{ J}$$

Calculate the work done against the constant resistance force $R = 13\text{ N}$:
$$W_R = R \times d = 13 \times 150 = 1950\text{ J}$$
$$W_D - W_R = 3600 - 1950 = 1650\text{ J}$$

Calculate the gravitational potential energy gained as the $84\text{ kg}$ athlete climbs the slope inclined at $0.8^\circ$:
$$\Delta E_p = mgd\sin 0.8^\circ = (84)(10)(150)\sin 0.8^\circ$$
$$84 \times 10 \times 150 = 126000$$
$$\sin 0.8^\circ \approx 0.01396219$$
$$\Delta E_p = 126000 \times 0.01396219 \approx 1759.236\text{ J}$$

Express the change in kinetic energy from initial speed $u = 3\text{ m s}^{-1}$ to final speed $v$:
$$\Delta E_k = \frac{1}{2}(84)v^2 - \frac{1}{2}(84)(3)^2 = 42v^2 - 42(9) = 42v^2 - 378$$

Set up the complete work-energy balance equation:
$$1650 = (42v^2 - 378) + 1759.236$$
$$1650 = 42v^2 + 1381.236$$

Subtract 1381.236 from both sides, then divide by 42:
$$42v^2 = 1650 - 1381.236 = 268.764$$
$$v^2 = \frac{268.764}{42} \approx 6.39914$$
$$v = \sqrt{6.39914} \approx 2.52965\text{ m s}^{-1}$$
$$v = 2.53\text{ m s}^{-1}\quad (\text{to 3 significant figures})$$
